Turn in: 1 PDF
Total: 100 points (5 parts × 20)

Required headings

  1. Sources
  2. Rules / Assumptions
  3. Work
  4. Check Your Answer
  5. One-Sentence Summary
Important: If you skip a heading, you may earn 0 for that part.

Weekly Chapters Schedule (Spring 2026)

Date Chapter Topic
Jan 20 1 Logic and Proofs
Jan 27 2 Sequences and Matrices
Feb 3 3 Algorithms
Feb 10 4 Cryptography
Feb 17 5 Recursion
Feb 24 6 Counting
Mar 3 7 Probability
Mar 10 8 Advanced Counting
Mar 24 9 Relations
Mar 31 10 Graphs
Apr 7 11 Trees
Apr 14 12 Boolean Algebra
Apr 21 13 Finite State Machines
Apr 28 — Farkle and Q-Learning

Pick one problem from this week’s chapter

You may choose any example or problem from the textbook, or you may modify one.
Cite where it came from (section/page or problem #). If you changed it, briefly explain what you changed and why.

1) Sources (20 pts)

Do: List 2 edited sources (textbook, class notes, university resource).
Add: 1 short bullet per source: what you used from it.

  • 20: 2+ edited sources + clear “I used this” bullets
  • 15: 2 sources but bullets are vague
  • 8: only 1 edited source
  • 0: no real sources

2) Rules / Assumptions (20 pts)

Do: Write the few rules you had to decide so the problem is clear.

Use this format:

  • Must-do (from prompt): ___
  • I will assume/decide: ___ (1–3 bullets)
  • 20: must-do + 1–3 clear decisions that make the task doable
  • 15: mostly clear but missing one key decision
  • 8: vague or too many unnecessary rules
  • 0: missing, or rules contradict the prompt

3) Work (20 pts)

Do: Show your steps clearly enough that someone else could follow.

  • 20: clear, correct steps
  • 15: mostly correct, small mistakes/gaps
  • 8: some work, but missing big steps
  • 0: little/no meaningful work

4) Check Your Answer (20 pts)

Do: Do one quick check and explain it (1–3 sentences).

Pick one:

  • small example / test case
  • edge case
  • compare to definition/theorem
  • sanity check (“does this make sense?”)
  • 20: one real check that could catch errors
  • 15: check exists but is weak
  • 8: “I think it’s right” (no real check)
  • 0: nothing

5) One-Sentence Summary (20 pts)

Do: In one sentence, say what the question asked you to do.

  • 20: accurate + specific
  • 15: mostly right but vague
  • 8: unclear or partly wrong
  • 0: missing

Quick self-check

  • ☐ 2 edited sources
  • ☐ 1–3 rules/assumptions
  • ☐ work shown
  • ☐ one check
  • ☐ one-sentence summary

A01: Unofficial transcript

Due: 2026-01-16

Generated from: 03_assignments/A01_unofficial_transcript/README.md

A01 — Unofficial transcript

Your unofficial transcript is the “receipt” of your college journey so far: - Transcript = what you’ve done - Progress report = what you still need - Degree plan = how you’re going to finish strong

What students will submit

Submit two files in Canvas:

1) Transcript PDF
- Export/download your Unofficial Transcript as a PDF - File name: - A01_Lastname_Firstname_UnofficialTranscript.pdf

2) Quick reflection (short write-up)
- A short reflection as PDF or Markdown - File name: - A01_Lastname_Firstname_TranscriptReflection.pdf - or A01_Lastname_Firstname_TranscriptReflection.md

Requirements

Part 1 — Get your unofficial transcript (PDF)

  1. Log in to Single Sign-On
  2. Open Self-Service
  3. Find Unofficial Transcript
  4. Download/export as PDF
  5. Confirm the PDF opens and looks readable (not blank, not sideways, not 1 pixel tall)
  6. You are looking at your Grade Point Average and making sure you can live with it or have a plan to fix it.
  7. Check for any transfer credit that should be there but is missing.
  8. Give it a vibe check for anything that feels off from your lived experience.

Part 2 — Reflection (answer all prompts)

In 5–10 sentences total, answer:

  1. What surprised you when you looked at your transcript?
  2. What’s one thing you’re proud of so far?
  3. What’s one thing you want to improve this semester (study habits, attendance, time management, asking for help, etc.)
  4. Any issues to flag (missing credit, repeated course, transfer credit weirdness, hold, incorrect grade posting)?

If you spot something that looks wrong, that’s not “bad news”—that’s useful intel. Bring it up early so we can fix it.

Privacy / safety rules (important)

  • Do not post your transcript anywhere public (GitHub, Discord, etc.)
  • Submit only through Canvas
  • If your transcript contains sensitive information (it often does), keep it private and don’t share it with classmates

Grading / rubric (10 points)

  • 4 pts — Transcript PDF submitted, readable, correct document
  • 4 pts — Reflection answers all prompts with real effort (not one-word responses)
  • 2 pts — File naming + submission is clean and on time

Common problems + fixes

  • “I can’t find the transcript option.”
    Try searching in Self-Service for: transcript and look for “unofficial transcript”.

  • “My transcript looks wrong.”
    Submit what you can and mention the issue in your reflection. We’ll handle it together.

  • “I have a hold and can’t access it.”

You’ll use your unofficial transcript, progress report, and the SWOSU catalog/schedule to map out your remaining semesters and confirm prerequisites + availability. But you need to connect the dots and come up with the semester you know you graduate.

This is a planning tool you should keep and update all semester (and bring to advising appointments). [And tape it to your wall to motivate you when you want to give up.]

Upload one PDF that was exported from a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets).

File naming

Example: - CS1_A03_DegreePlan_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fa.pdf

Requirements (what must be in your spreadsheet)

1) Title + basics (top of page)

Include: - Your name - Major (and minor if applicable) - Option (if applicable) - Your expected graduation semester (example: “Spring 2028”)

2) Semester-by-semester plan (the main table)

Your plan must list every semester from now until graduation.

For each planned course, include: - Course prefix/number (example: CS 1033) - Course name (example: “Computer Science I”) - Credits - Notes (optional but encouraged: “needs prereq,” “only offered fall,” etc.)

For each semester, include: - Total credits that semester

3) Prerequisites + reality check

Somewhere on the sheet (or in a notes area), show evidence that you checked: - SWOSU course catalog / schedule offerings (when courses are typically offered) - Your progress report (what requirements remain) - Your unofficial transcript (what you already completed)

This can be: - A short “checked list” section - Notes in a dedicated column - A small “Verification” box

For each scenario, clearly show: - Expected graduation term - What changes between the two plans (credit load / summer / specific course shifts)

5) Advising notes / questions

A04 — Resume (Professional Artifact + Evidence Pack)

Due: SET_THIS

P01 — Resume (Professional Artifact + Evidence Pack)

Your resume is not a history report. It’s a marketing document with one purpose:

To convince a hiring manager to interview you.

This assignment is a full professional build: you will create a resume that follows modern best practices, targets a real job or internship, and includes an “evidence pack” proving your claims are real and intentional.

What you will submit (Canvas)

Submit THREE files:

1) Resume PDF
- Filename: A04_Lastname_Firstname_Resume.pdf

2) Evidence Pack (PDF)
- Filename: A04_Lastname_Firstname_EvidencePack.pdf

3) Reflection + Revision Log (PDF or Markdown)
- Filename: A04_Lastname_Firstname_RevisionLog.pdf (or .md)

Part A — Choose a target (required)

Pick one real posting you could qualify for within 0–3 years: - internship / student worker / entry-level job

In your Revision Log, include: - Job title + company - A link to the posting (or a screenshot if needed) - 5 keywords or skill phrases from the posting

Example keywords: - “customer service” - “Python” - “troubleshooting” - “team collaboration” - “documentation” - “data analysis” - “networking basics” - “Excel / spreadsheets” - “public speaking” - “project management”

Part B — Resume requirements (you must meet these)

1) Format and structure rules (non-negotiable)

  • 1 page (unless you have 10+ years of relevant experience—rare)
  • Single-column layout (ATS-friendly; avoid multi-column templates)
  • Consistent spacing, fonts, and alignment
  • Clear section headings (as applicable):
  • Education, Experience, Projects, Skills, Certifications/Awards
  • Bullet points (not paragraphs) for Experience/Projects

2) Required sections

Your resume must include:

Header - Name - City/State - Phone - Professional email - LinkedIn URL (or “LinkedIn: In progress” if not yet created)

Education - School, degree/major (or intended major), expected graduation date - GPA optional (include only if strong and accurate)

Experience You must include at least one: - job, volunteer role, internship, leadership role, or meaningful responsibility

Projects You must include at least one project (class, personal, club, work).
Projects count even if you think they’re “small.”

Skills - 8–16 skills, grouped into categories - Example: Languages, Tools, Concepts, Professional Skills

3) Bullet point quality rules (this is where you earn points)

You must write: - 8–12 bullets total across Experience + Projects
- At least 6 bullets must follow this formula:

Action Verb + What you did + How you did it + Result/Impact

Strong bullet examples (copy the pattern, not the content)

  • Improved a spreadsheet-based inventory tracker by automating formulas and validation, reducing data entry errors from frequent mistakes to rare ones.
  • Built a Python program that parses and summarizes text files using functions and loops; delivered results in a clean table format.
  • Led a 4-person lab team by assigning roles and setting checkpoints, finishing 2 days early with all requirements met.
  • Resolved customer issues by asking diagnostic questions and documenting outcomes, maintaining positive feedback (use numbers if you have them).

Weak bullet examples (avoid these)

  • “Responsible for helping customers.”
  • “Worked on a project in class.”
  • “Did programming in Python.”
  • “Good communication skills.”

4) Proof and credibility rules

  • No inflated titles, no fake metrics, no “expert” if you’re not.
  • If you use numbers, they must be real or clearly described as approximate.
  • Every bullet should be something you can explain out loud.

Part C — Evidence Pack (this is how you prove it)

Create a PDF with evidence backing your resume claims.

Include at least 6 items, chosen from below (mix is encouraged): - Screenshot of a project README, GitHub repo page, or code snippet - Photo of a poster/presentation you made - Screenshot of a spreadsheet/dashboard you built - Certificate (LinkedIn Learning, etc.) - Email or note showing recognition (blur names if needed) - A short “before/after” example of something you improved - A work sample excerpt (documentation, tutorial you wrote, lab report section)

Rules: - If it’s sensitive, blur/black out private info. - The Evidence Pack must have a table of contents: - Item #, title, and which resume bullet it supports (e.g., “Supports Bullet 3”)

Part D — Reflection + revision log (required)

In 1–2 pages total, answer:

1) Your resume’s message (the “headline”)
In one sentence: What do you want a hiring manager to believe about you?
Example: “I’m a reliable early-career tech professional who learns fast, communicates clearly, and finishes projects.”

2) Your best 3 bullets and why they’re strong
Explain using the formula: action + method + impact.

3) Your weakest section and your plan to strengthen it
Be specific: “Add a second project,” “Join Computer Club,” “Complete a certificate,” etc.

4) Revision record
- Include two rounds of revision - Describe what changed each time (formatting, verbs, metrics, clarity) - If you used AI: state how you used it (example: “I used AI to rewrite bullets, then edited to match my real experience.”)

AI / internet tools policy (allowed—with ownership)

You may use AI/LLMs and online examples to: - generate bullet drafts - reword for clarity - suggest formats or action verbs

But: - Your resume must be accurate and personal - If asked, you must be able to explain or edit any bullet - Generic, copy-paste-looking content will lose points on quality

Privacy / safety rules (important)

  • Do not post your resume publicly (GitHub, Discord, etc.) unless you intentionally choose to later
  • Do not include sensitive info (SSN, full address, birthdate, etc.)
  • Submit only through Canvas

Grading rubric (Likert-style) — 100 points total

How grading works: Each category below is scored 0–4 based on the descriptors.
Points are then calculated using the category weight.

Category points = (score ÷ 4) × category weight

Example: If “Bullet Quality” is weight 30 and the student earns a 3:
(3/4) × 30 = 22.5 points.

1) Format + ATS readiness (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
1 page, single-column, clean headings, consistent spacing/fonts, no clutter. Reads easily in 10 seconds. ATS-friendly.

3 — Mostly (11.25):
Mostly clean and readable; minor formatting issues (slightly inconsistent spacing, headings, or alignment) but still ATS-friendly.

2 — Some (7.5):
Formatting distracts from content: inconsistent headings/spacing, dense sections, awkward layout. Still readable but not professional.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Hard to read or clearly not ATS-friendly: multi-column template, tiny font, clutter, or confusing organization.

0 — No credit (0):
Not submitted, not a resume, or unreadable file.

2) Targeting to a real posting (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
Posting link (or screenshot) included; 5 keywords listed; resume clearly reflects the posting (skills/bullets aligned).

3 — Mostly (11.25):
Posting + keywords included; some alignment, but targeting is uneven (keywords don’t show up in bullets/skills strongly).

2 — Some (7.5):
Posting OR keywords are weak/missing detail; resume looks generic; minimal connection to the job requirements.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Posting is unclear/unrelated; keywords missing; targeting not attempted.

0 — No credit (0):
No posting and no keywords; completely ignores this requirement.

3) Required sections complete (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
Header, Education, Experience, Projects, Skills all present and meaningful. Skills are grouped and specific.

3 — Mostly (11.25):
All sections present but one is thin (e.g., projects vague or skills not grouped) OR minor missing detail.

2 — Some (7.5):
One required section missing OR multiple sections are too thin/vague to be useful.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Two+ required sections missing; looks incomplete or rushed.

0 — No credit (0):
Not a resume or not submitted.

4) Bullet quality + best practices (Weight: 30)

4 — Full credit (30):
8–12 bullets total. At least 6 bullets follow Action + Method + Impact. Strong verbs, specific tools, no filler. Bullets are believable and clear.

3 — Mostly (22.5):
Meets bullet count; several strong bullets, but impact/method is missing in a few. Some generic wording remains.

2 — Some (15):
Bullets exist but many are weak (“responsible for,” vague duties, no tools, no outcomes). Less than 6 strong-formula bullets.

1 — Not yet (7.5):
Few bullets, mostly vague or task-only statements. Little evidence of best practices.

0 — No credit (0):
No bullets, or bullet content is clearly unrelated / copied without understanding.

5) Evidence Pack quality + mapping (Weight: 15)

4 — Full credit (15):
6+ evidence items, table of contents included, each item clearly maps to a resume bullet (“supports bullet #”). Evidence is relevant and professional.

3 — Mostly (11.25):
6 items present with a TOC, but mapping is sometimes unclear OR some items are weak evidence.

2 — Some (7.5):
Fewer than 6 items OR missing TOC OR mapping to bullets is inconsistent/confusing.

1 — Not yet (3.75):
Evidence pack is mostly filler, unrelated, or not clearly connected to resume claims.

0 — No credit (0):
No evidence pack submitted.

6) Reflection + revision log (Weight: 10)

4 — Full credit (10):
Includes: resume “message” sentence, best 3 bullets explained using best-practice logic, weakest section + plan, and two revision rounds described. If AI used, explains how.

3 — Mostly (7.5):
Covers most requirements; missing one piece (e.g., only one revision round or weak explanation of bullet strength).

2 — Some (5):
Reflection is brief or generic; revision details unclear; missing multiple required parts.

1 — Not yet (2.5):
Minimal effort; doesn’t demonstrate understanding of what was improved and why.

0 — No credit (0):
Not submitted.

LLM-friendly feedback format (optional but recommended)

When giving feedback, include: 1) Category scores (0–4)
2) 2–3 bullets of “what you did well”
3) 2–3 bullets of “highest-impact fixes next”
4) Rewrite one weak bullet into a strong bullet (Action + Method + Impact)

Suggested Canvas settings (edit if needed)

  • Available: Week 2 Monday, 12:00am (suggestion)
  • Due: Week 2 Thursday, 5:00pm (suggestion)
  • Until: End of semester, 11:59pm
  • Points: 100
  • Submission type: File upload (PDFs) + file upload or text entry for Revision Log

Dream Job Report (Role Research + Personal Motivation)

A05 — Dream Job Report (Role Research + Personal Motivation)

Due: SET_THIS

P02 — Dream Job Report (Role Research + Personal Motivation)

This is the professional mirror of the degree-plan work you did at the start of the semester.

  • Your resume = your “unofficial transcript” (what’s true today)
  • Your dream job report = your professional “degree plan” (where you want to go and what that role actually requires)

Goal: Identify a real role you want to grow into, understand what it demands, and explain why it matters to you. This is not fantasy — it’s future planning.

Why this assignment exists (read this first)

A dream job report is a motivation engine and a navigation map.

  • It helps you decide what you’re aiming at (so you don’t wander for four years and then wonder why job searching feels impossible).
  • It turns “someday” into a concrete target: responsibilities, tools, expectations, and what success looks like.
  • It becomes the foundation for the next assignment: your Gap Analysis (what you still need and how you’ll build it).

Important mindset: This is a target, not a judgment.
You are not expected to be ready for this job today. You are expected to be honest, specific, and intentional.

Also: this is one of the few assignments that is primarily about you — it’s designed to be private and personally useful.

What you will submit (Canvas)

Submit using TWO Canvas submission parts:

Part 1 — File Upload (required)

Upload TWO PDFs:

1) Dream Job Report (PDF)
Filename: A05_Lastname_Firstname_DreamJobReport.pdf

2) Job Posting Snapshot + Source List (PDF)
Filename: A05_Lastname_Firstname_JobSources.pdf

Part 2 — Text Entry (required)

Paste the full text of your Dream Job Report into the Canvas Text Entry box.

Why this is required: PDF is a layout format and sometimes text can be extracted in weird order by automated tools. Pasting the text ensures you get the best possible feedback from automated review tools and makes your submission easier to read and review.

(Yes — you still upload the PDF. The Text Entry is for clean text and feedback.)

LLM-friendly formatting rules (required)

To make your PDF readable to both humans and automated tools:

  • Use a single-column layout
  • Avoid text boxes, sidebars, and fancy templates
  • Keep tables short (a small table is fine; don’t put your whole report in a table)
  • Export a normal PDF with selectable text (not a scanned image)

Part A — Pick a real dream job + a realistic backup (required)

Choose one specific job title you would be excited to hold in 5–10 years.

Also choose a backup plan role (Plan B) that still interests you and is closer to entry-level.

Rules for job selection

  • It must be a real job title found in real postings (company site, LinkedIn, Indeed, USAJobs, etc.).
  • “Entrepreneur / business owner” is not a job title for this assignment.
    If your dream is to run a business, choose the functional role you would do most days.

Examples: - Founder — Engineering Lead - Founder — Product & Sales - Founder — Operations / Finance - Founder — Cybersecurity Consultant

Your responsibilities/tools/metrics must match that function (no fluffy “I will inspire people” job descriptions — real work only).

Part B — Collect evidence (required sources)

You must use at least 3 credible sources.
At least 1 source must be from this “high-trust” list: - BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook (OOH) (government career profiles: duties, environment, education/training, pay, outlook) - USAJOBS (official federal job postings) - An official company job posting (company careers page)

Other credible sources you may use: - Professional organizations (ACM, IEEE, ISACA, etc.) - Certification providers (CompTIA, Cisco, AWS, Microsoft, PMI, etc.) - University career services pages - Handshake/LinkedIn Learning course pages (as supporting info)

Your JobSources PDF must include

  • 1–2 job postings (screenshots or saved PDFs)
  • A source list with working links AND a 1–2 sentence note describing what each source contributed

Citations (simple, consistent)

Use any citation style you want (APA/MLA/Chicago/etc.), but be consistent.
At minimum, include working links and source notes.

Part C — Write your Dream Job Report (main deliverable)

Length: 2–3 pages (double-spaced)
Format: 12 pt font, 1-inch margins, clear section headings
Tone: professional but personal — this should motivate you

Use the headings below in this order.

1) Job Identity (who/what/where)

Include: - Dream Job Title (Plan A) - Backup Job Title (Plan B) - Typical industries or employers - Work setting (remote/on-site/hybrid, team size, environment) - A 3–5 sentence “day-in-the-life” summary (based on sources)

2) Job Description (what you actually do)

Write a job description in your own words (not copied). Include:

  • 6–10 core responsibilities
  • 5 key tools/technologies (or methods) used in the role
  • 3 success metrics (how performance is measured)

Examples of success metrics (pick ones that fit your role): - “Reduce incidents / downtime” - “Deliver features on schedule” - “Improve performance by X%” - “Customer satisfaction / ticket resolution time” - “Accuracy / error rate / reliability” - “Security findings reduced / compliance maintained”

3) Requirements Map (what the job expects)

Create a simple table (include in your report):

Requirement Type Plan A: What the job requires Evidence/source
Education
Technical Skills
Professional Skills
Experience
Certifications (if relevant)

Then add a second mini-table for Plan B:

Requirement Type Plan B: What the job requires Evidence/source
Education
Technical Skills
Professional Skills
Experience
Certifications (if relevant)

4) Why this is your dream job (the motivation engine)

Answer honestly: - Why does this role excite you? - What problems do you want to solve? - What impact do you want to have (people, community, business, science, etc.)?

Reminder: This is a target, not a judgment. Be real. Be specific.

5) Fit Check (what you already have + what you still need)

Write two short lists for Plan A:

Already building (at least 5 items):
Skills, strengths, experiences, habits, or values you already have that support this path.

Still need to build (at least 5 items):
Skills, credentials, experiences, or habits you must develop to be competitive.

Then add a short note: - Which gaps overlap between Plan A and Plan B? - Which gaps are unique to Plan A?

6) How you combined sources (anti-copy/paste paragraph)

Write a short paragraph (5–8 sentences) answering: - Which sources you used - What each source helped you understand - How you combined them into your own job description and requirements map

This is a simple way to show honest effort and reduce accidental copy/paste.

7) Your 12-month action plan (first step toward the future)

Create a concrete plan with 8–12 actions you can take in the next year.

Your plan must include: - 2 actions related to coursework - 2 actions related to projects/portfolio - 2 actions related to professional networking or involvement (club, event, mentorship, etc.) - 1 action related to communication (writing, speaking, presenting, interviewing) - 1 action related to skill-building (course/certification/self-study)

Make each action specific (recommended format): - Verb + artifact + deadline
Examples: - “Build a small data project and publish a README by April 1.” - “Attend one Computer Club meeting and introduce myself to 2 members by Feb 15.” - “Complete one LinkedIn Learning course on interviewing by March 10.”

Put your plan in checklist format and include a timeline (this semester / summer / next fall).

AI / internet tools policy (allowed — with ownership)

You may use AI/LLMs to: - help outline your report - improve clarity and writing - summarize sources (then verify)

But: - You must write in your own voice - Do not copy job postings word-for-word - If your report reads generic or source-copied, you will lose points on quality - You should be able to explain your choices and revise a section if asked

Grading rubric (Likert-style) — 100 points total

How grading works: Each category is scored 0–4.
Points = (score ÷ 4) × category weight.

1) Job selection + clarity (Plan A + Plan B) (Weight: 15)

4: Plan A and Plan B are real, specific roles; time horizon makes sense; titles are precise and consistent; founder roles have clear functional focus.
3: Roles are real but slightly vague or Plan B is weakly defined.
2: Role selection is fuzzy, inconsistent, or unrealistic; Plan B unclear.
1: Very vague (“work with computers”), unclear roles or missing Plan B.
0: Not real job titles / off-task.

2) Evidence + source quality (Weight: 20)

4: 3+ credible sources; includes 1–2 postings; includes at least 1 high-trust source; clear source notes; evidence supports claims.
3: Sources credible but notes are thin OR postings missing one required item OR high-trust source is present but weakly used.
2: Weak sources or unclear contributions; postings limited; high-trust requirement barely met.
1: Minimal sources; credibility concerns; little evidence used.
0: No sources / missing JobSources PDF.

3) Job description quality (responsibilities/tools/metrics) (Weight: 20)

4: Responsibilities/tools/metrics are specific, accurate, and clearly written in student’s own words; reads like a real job.
3: Mostly specific; some vague items; metrics/tools not strongly connected.
2: Generic description; unclear responsibilities; tools/metrics weak.
1: Mostly copied tone or very unclear.
0: Missing.

4) Requirements Map quality (Plan A + Plan B) (Weight: 15)

4: Both tables complete; evidence column filled; covers education, tech/pro skills, experience, certs (if relevant).
3: Both tables present but evidence is weak for some items OR one table thinner.
2: Tables incomplete or too generic; missing categories or evidence.
1: Bare minimum effort; not useful.
0: Missing.

5) Motivation + personal connection (Weight: 15)

4: Authentic, specific, meaningful; connects values, impact, and reasons clearly; motivating to read.
3: Personal connection present but could be deeper or more specific.
2: Generic motivation; limited reflection.
1: Minimal personal connection.
0: Missing.

6) Fit Check + reflection on gaps (Weight: 5)

4: 5+ items in each list; thoughtful; clearly identifies overlap vs unique gaps.
3: Lists complete but somewhat generic; overlap/unique note thin.
2: Lists too short or vague; weak analysis.
1: Minimal effort.
0: Missing.

7) Source-combination paragraph (Weight: 5)

4: Clearly explains how sources were combined; shows honest synthesis; reduces copy/paste risk.
3: Present but shallow; limited synthesis detail.
2: Very brief; unclear how sources were used.
1: Minimal effort.
0: Missing.

8) 12-month action plan quality (Weight: 15)

4: 8–12 actions; meets all required categories; includes timeline; actions are concrete (verb + artifact + deadline).
3: Meets most requirements; a few actions vague or missing one category/timeline detail.
2: Too few actions; vague; missing multiple categories.
1: Minimal plan; not actionable.
0: Missing.

Submission checklist

Before submitting, confirm: - [ ] Report is 2–3 pages, double-spaced, with the required headings (in order) - [ ] Both Requirements Map tables are included and filled out with evidence - [ ] Source-combination paragraph is included - [ ] 12-month action plan includes 8–12 concrete actions + timeline - [ ] JobSources PDF includes 1–2 postings + 3+ sources + notes + at least 1 high-trust source - [ ] You uploaded PDFs AND pasted your report text into the Canvas Text Entry box

Suggested Canvas settings (edit if needed)

  • Available: Week 3 Monday, 12:00am (suggestion)
  • Due: Week 3 Thursday, 5:00pm (suggestion)
  • Until: End of semester, 11:59pm
  • Points: 100
  • Submission type: File upload + Text Entry

A06 — Professional Gap Analysis (Career Trajectory Plan)

Due: SET_THIS

A06 — Professional Gap Analysis (Career Trajectory Plan)

This is the professional version of your semester-by-semester degree plan — but for your career.

  • Resume (A04) = where you are now (your “professional transcript”)
  • Dream Job Report (A05) = where you want to be (your target role + requirements)
  • Gap Analysis (A06) = how you will close the gap with a realistic plan

Goal: Identify what you need to become competitive for your dream job, be honest about where you are today, and build a concrete action plan that proves you’re taking your career seriously.

This is not about perfection — it’s about direction, strategy, and momentum.

What you will submit (Canvas)

Submit using TWO Canvas submission parts:

Part 1 — File Upload (required)

Upload ONE PDF:

  • Gap Analysis Report (PDF)
    Filename: A06_Lastname_Firstname_GapAnalysis.pdf

Part 2 — Text Entry (required)

Paste the full text of your Gap Analysis Report into the Canvas Text Entry box.

Why: Your PDF is the official artifact. The pasted text helps automated feedback tools read your work cleanly and give better recommendations.
Note: Many companies use automated tools to screen candidates and documents. Learning to format clearly and plan ahead is part of becoming job-ready.

LLM-friendly formatting rules (required)

  • Use a single-column layout
  • Avoid text boxes, sidebars, and fancy templates
  • Keep tables short (tables are fine; don’t embed your entire report inside one)
  • Export a normal PDF with selectable text (not a scanned image)

Before you start (required inputs)

You must use information from: - Your Dream Job Report (A05) (Plan A + Plan B roles and requirements) - Your Resume (A04) (your current evidence)

If you change your dream job since A05, that’s allowed — but you must clearly explain why in Section 1.

Your Gap Analysis Report (main deliverable)

Length: 2–4 pages (double-spaced)
Format: 12 pt font, 1-inch margins, clear section headings
Tone: professional and honest — this is your roadmap

Use the sections below in this order.

1) Career Target Snapshot (Plan A + Plan B)

Include: - Plan A job title + 1–2 sentence “why this role” - Plan B job title + 1–2 sentence “why this backup role” - 6–10 keywords pulled from your A05 sources (skills/tools/traits employers ask for)

2) Skill Categories (the full map)

You will analyze your gaps across six categories:

  1. Technical / Tools
  2. Core Concepts (what you understand)
  3. Projects / Portfolio Evidence
  4. Experience (work, internships, leadership, volunteering, labs)
  5. Professional Skills (communication, teamwork, reliability, leadership)
  6. Network + Opportunity (clubs, professional orgs, mentors, events, internships)

Why this matters: Taking one class is not the same as being job-ready.
A class can help, but employers look for proof: projects, practice, and experience.

3) Rating scale (required anchors)

You will rate your Current level and your Target level for each item using this scale:

  • 1 — No experience: I have not done this.
  • 2 — Minimal exposure: I’ve seen it, but I can’t do it yet.
  • 3 — Assisted competence: I can do it with notes, examples, or help.
  • 4 — Independent competence: I can do it on my own reliably.
  • 5 — Mastery: I can teach it, troubleshoot it, and explain it clearly.

Proof rule (important)

If you rate yourself 4 or 5, you must include specific evidence (an artifact or experience) that supports it.

Examples of acceptable evidence: - a project repo + README - an assignment name + what you built - a certificate - a job task you did repeatedly - a presentation/demo you gave - a club leadership role with clear responsibilities

4) The Gap Table (required)

Create a table with at least 12 rows total.
Include both hard skills and soft skills, and include items from multiple categories above.

Use a 1–5 scale where Gap = Target − Current.

Gap Table Template

Category Skill / Requirement (must be specific/testable) Current (1–5) Target (1–5) Gap Evidence I can point to today (artifact/experience) How I will close the gap (specific action)
Technical/Tools
Concepts
Projects
Experience
Professional Skills
Network/Opportunity

Rules (to prevent weak tables)

  • 12 rows minimum
  • No umbrella skills. Each row must be testable/specific.
  • Bad: “Python”
  • Better: “Python: write functions, parse files, use lists/dicts, debug with print/logging”
  • Bad: “Databases”
  • Better: “SQL: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY; design a simple schema”
  • No duplicates. You cannot list the same skill 3 different ways.
  • At least 2 rows must be Network + Opportunity
  • At least 2 rows must be Projects/Portfolio
  • At least 2 rows must be Professional Skills
  • At least 4 rows must be Technical/Concepts
  • Evidence must be real and specific — not “I think I’m good at it.”

5) Prioritize the Top Gaps (the 80/20 section)

Pick your top 5 highest-impact gaps (not necessarily the biggest number — the most important for employability).

Required mix (so you don’t pick only easy gaps)

Your Top 5 must include: - 2 from Technical/Concepts - 1 from Projects/Portfolio - 1 from Experience - 1 from Network + Opportunity

For each top gap, write a short paragraph that answers: - Why this gap matters for Plan A (and whether it matters for Plan B) - What “proof” would look like on your resume (a bullet point you could eventually write) - The fastest realistic way to close it this year

Impact test (use this):
“If I close this gap, does it produce a new resume bullet or unlock better internship/job opportunities?”

6) Your Close-the-Gap Plan (12-month roadmap)

Make a plan with 12–18 actions you can take in the next year.

Your plan must include:

  • 3 coursework actions (each must include a deliverable)
    Example format: course + artifact + deadline
  • “In Database Systems, build a schema + queries project and publish a short report by May 1.”
  • 3 portfolio/project actions (deliverable required: repo/README/demo/report)
  • 2 internship/experience actions (apply/track, campus job, lab role, volunteering, shadowing)
  • 2 networking actions (Computer Club, professional society, event, career fair, guest talk)
  • 2 communication actions (presentation, mock interview, writing sample, documentation habit)
  • 2 skill-building actions (LinkedIn Learning, certification, structured self-study plan)
  • 1 “adulting the job search” action (LinkedIn cleanup, Handshake profile, resume review appointment, etc.)

Realism rule (important)

Your plan should average 1–2 meaningful actions per month while you are a full-time student.

Momentum rule (recommended)

Include 3 “small win” actions that can be done in 60 minutes or less (to build momentum).

Make actions specific (recommended format)

Verb + artifact + deadline Examples: - “Complete a LinkedIn Learning course on Excel and add the certificate by March 15.” - “Build a small database project and publish a README + screenshots by April 10.” - “Attend 2 Computer Club meetings and talk to 2 members each time by Feb 28.” - “Apply to 5 internships and track outcomes in a spreadsheet by April 1.”

Put your plan as a checklist and include a timeline: this semester / summer / next fall.

7) Reality Check: “Taking a class is not mastery” (required reflection)

Write 1–2 paragraphs responding to this prompt:

Explain why taking a class is not the same as being job-ready, and describe what additional proof you will build beyond coursework (projects, practice, experience, networking).

To avoid a generic answer, include: - One skill you currently rate as a 3 and what proof would move it to a 4 - One job requirement you used to underestimate, and what you’ll do about it

8) Optional (bonus but powerful): One-page “Resume Additions” preview

Write 3 resume bullets you expect to be able to add by the end of this semester if you follow your plan.

Use the strong bullet formula: Action + Method + Impact

AI / internet tools policy (allowed — with ownership)

You may use AI/LLMs to: - brainstorm gaps based on your dream job requirements - improve clarity of writing - help turn vague actions into concrete steps

But: - Your ratings must be honest and defensible - Your evidence must be real - Your plan must be specific and achievable - Generic “I will learn everything” plans will lose points

Privacy / safety note

This document can contain personal goals and plans. It is intended to be private and used to support you — not to be posted publicly.

Grading rubric (Likert-style) — 100 points total

How grading works: Each category is scored 0–4.
Points = (score ÷ 4) × category weight.

1) Career target clarity (Plan A + Plan B) (Weight: 10)

4: Both roles are clear, realistic, and consistent with prior work; keywords included.
3: Roles clear but Plan B is weak or keywords thin.
2: Roles fuzzy, unrealistic, or inconsistent; keywords weak.
1: Very vague roles or missing Plan B.
0: Off-task / missing.

2) Gap Table quality (completeness + specificity + honesty) (Weight: 30)

4: 12+ rows; balanced categories; no umbrella skills/duplicates; ratings make sense; evidence is specific; “close the gap” actions are concrete; proof rule used for 4–5 ratings.
3: Meets minimum; minor issues (some vague rows, thin evidence, or weak actions).
2: Too few rows OR categories missing OR vague skills/duplicates OR ratings feel unjustified.
1: Minimal effort; mostly vague; weak connection to real evidence.
0: Missing table.

3) Top 5 gaps (impact + required mix) (Weight: 20)

4: High-impact; meets required mix; includes proof targets (resume bullets) and fast realistic strategies; connects to Plan A/Plan B.
3: Good gaps; mostly meets mix; analysis somewhat generic or Plan B connection thin.
2: Gaps not high-impact OR missing required mix OR shallow strategies.
1: Minimal or unclear.
0: Missing.

4) 12-month roadmap (specificity + coverage + realism) (Weight: 30)

4: 12–18 actions; meets all required categories; coursework actions include deliverables; actions are concrete (verb+artifact+deadline); timeline included; includes small wins; realistic pacing.
3: Meets most requirements; a few actions vague or missing one requirement (small wins, deliverables, or a category).
2: Too few actions; vague; missing multiple categories or deliverables.
1: Minimal plan; not actionable.
0: Missing.

5) Reality-check reflection (Weight: 10)

4: Clear exposure vs competence explanation; includes the required “3→4 proof” and underestimated requirement; thoughtful and honest.
3: Present but somewhat generic; missing one required detail.
2: Shallow or unclear; missing required details.
1: Minimal effort.
0: Missing.

Submission checklist

Before submitting, confirm: - [ ] PDF uploaded with correct filename - [ ] Report text pasted into Canvas Text Entry - [ ] Gap Table has 12+ rows and meets all category minimums - [ ] No umbrella skills and no duplicate rows - [ ] Any 4–5 rating has real evidence listed - [ ] Top 5 gaps meet the required category mix and include proof targets - [ ] 12–18 action plan meets all required action types and includes deadlines + timeline - [ ] Reflection includes the required “3→4 proof” and underestimated requirement

Suggested Canvas settings (edit if needed)

  • Available: Week 4 Monday, 12:00am (suggestion)
  • Due: Week 4 Thursday, 5:00pm (suggestion)
  • Until: End of semester, 11:59pm
  • Points: 100
  • Submission type: File upload + Text Entry
