pages.title: The Pomodoro Method — Springtime Sprints for Focus
pages.body:
Tomato Timer Method (Supplement)

Generated from: 02_weeks\W01\04_tomato_timer_method_supliment.md

The Pomodoro Method — Springtime Sprints for Focus

0) Big Idea (the whole method in one breath)

The Pomodoro Method is a way to do focused work in short sprints, take deliberate breaks, and repeat—so your brain stays sharp instead of turning into a sizzling CPU with no heatsink.

Classic rhythm: - 25 minutes focused work
- 5 minutes break
- After 4 rounds, take a longer break (15–30 minutes)

But the real secret is not the timer.
It’s the agreement you make with yourself: “For this short window, I do one thing.”

1) Why it’s called “Pomodoro” (and what that has to do with springtime sprints)

“Pomodoro” is Italian for tomato. The method is named after the tomato-shaped kitchen timer used by its creator while studying.

So why do I call it “springtime sprints”? - Spring is when things start again—fresh growth, fresh momentum, fresh habits. - Pomodoro is the same energy: not an endless grind, but a sequence of short, renewable bursts. - You’re not trying to “win the semester” in one heroic night. You’re trying to win the next 25 minutes—over and over—until the semester bends to your will.

The tomato timer is the mascot; the sprint mentality is the magic.

2) Why it was developed (what problem it was trying to solve)

Pomodoro was developed to solve a very human problem:

“I know what I should do… but I can’t start… and when I start, I don’t stay… and when I drift, I feel guilty… and then I avoid it more.”

It’s a method built for: - Overwhelm (the task feels too big) - Avoidance (starting feels painful) - Drift (you sit down and your brain escapes out the ventilation shaft) - Perfectionism (you keep “preparing” instead of doing) - Time confusion (“I’ve been working for hours!” — no, you’ve been near work for hours)

Pomodoro shrinks “the task” into a time box.
You don’t promise to finish the entire project.
You promise to attack it for one sprint.

3) Why anxiety, stress, and distraction became the problem (and why it’s worse now)

People have always procrastinated. But modern life pours rocket fuel on it.

3.1 Anxiety: too many consequences, too little certainty

Students often carry: - grade pressure - financial pressure - family pressure - future-career pressure - “I must not fail” pressure

Anxiety doesn’t just make you feel bad—it reduces working memory. That means you have fewer mental “registers” available for problem-solving.

3.1.1 What anxiety really is (in human terms)

Anxiety is your brain doing threat math: - “What could go wrong?” - “How bad would it be?” - “Can I handle it?” - “Will I be alone if I mess up?”

When the brain decides the stakes are high and the outcome is uncertain, it flips into protection mode. Protection mode is good for avoiding bears. It is not great for writing proofs, debugging code, having hard conversations, or learning anything that requires flexible thinking.

3.1.2 Why anxiety has gotten louder

A few forces crank the volume up for humans in general, not just students:

  • More visible comparison We used to compare ourselves to a small circle (friends, neighbors, coworkers). Now we compare ourselves to highlight reels of the entire planet. Even if you “know it’s curated,” your nervous system still treats it as competition.

  • More uncertainty in the basics Housing costs, healthcare, job stability, retirement—many people feel like the floor is less solid than it used to be. When the basics feel wobbly, the brain becomes more sensitive to risk everywhere else.

  • Always-on expectations Notifications, Slack, email, texts—there’s a constant sense of “I should be reachable.” Reachability quietly becomes responsibility. Responsibility turns into pressure. Pressure turns into anxiety.

  • Too many choices, too few clear paths More options can mean more freedom—but also more fear of picking wrong. Humans hate irreversible decisions under uncertainty.

3.1.3 The major pressure types (and where they come from)

This is the same set of pressures, whether you’re 19 or 49:

  • Performance pressure (grades, metrics, status) Comes from systems that reward outcomes more than learning. Humans start believing “my value = my results.”

  • Survival pressure (money, health, housing) Comes from real-world constraints. It’s not weakness—it’s realism. But survival pressure narrows attention and increases avoidance when tasks feel risky.

  • Belonging pressure (family, peers, identity) Humans are wired to stay connected to the group. Anxiety often whispers: “If I fail, I’ll be rejected.”

  • Future pressure (career, meaning, time) This is the “clock pressure”: “I’m behind.” “I’m wasting my potential.” “I’m running out of time.” Even when life is objectively okay, this pressure can still bite.

  • Perfection pressure (“I must not fail”) Often learned from environments where mistakes were punished, mocked, or remembered forever. Perfectionism is usually fear wearing a tuxedo.

3.1.4 What anxiety does to the mind (why it wrecks focus)

When anxiety rises: - working memory shrinks (fewer “mental registers” available) - the brain seeks quick certainty (easy tasks, easy rewards) - ambiguity feels painful (so complex tasks get avoided) - you become more distractible (because scanning for threats is the priority)

This is why someone can be intelligent and motivated… and still “can’t start.”

3.1.5 Common triggers we accidentally create in other people

A lot of anxiety spikes aren’t caused by the work itself—they’re caused by the social environment around the work.

Common trigger patterns: - Vague expectations (“Just do a good job.”) - Unclear success criteria (people don’t know what “done” means) - Surprise consequences (gotcha grading, hidden rules, sudden penalties) - Public comparison (leaderboards, calling out mistakes in front of others) - Time ambiguity (“Sometime soon.” / “ASAP.”) - High-stakes language (“This is make-or-break.”) - Unstable feedback (inconsistent standards, mood-based responses) - No safe path to recover (mistakes feel permanent)

Humans can tolerate hard work. What they struggle with is hard work + uncertainty + shame risk.

3.1.6 How to reduce anxiety triggers in others (without going soft)

This is the “be kind and effective” toolkit.

1) Make success visible - Provide examples of “good enough,” “strong,” and “excellent.” - Use rubrics, checklists, or short acceptance criteria. - Say: “Here’s what I’m looking for.”

2) Make the next step small When someone is anxious, “the project” is too big. Offer the first bite: - “Open the file.” - “Write the function header.” - “Run the starter tests.” - “List 3 assumptions.”

3) Separate person from performance Use language that protects identity: - “This draft needs work” (not “You’re not good at this”) - “This is a skill” (not “This is who you are”)

4) Normalize mistakes as data Especially in technical work: - “Bugs are information.” - “Incorrect proofs are stepping stones.” - “Failed tests are the flashlight, not the verdict.”

5) Reduce surprise penalties If consequences must exist, make them predictable. Surprise is rocket fuel for anxiety.

6) Give private correction, public encouragement If someone’s error becomes a public event, they’ll avoid trying next time.

7) Offer a recovery plan Anxiety calms when people know: - “If I mess up, here’s how I get back on track.” Examples: - revision tokens - resubmission windows - partial credit for process artifacts - “checkpoint” deadlines before the final

8) Use calmer time language Swap “ASAP” with: - “By end of day” - “Before class on Thursday” - “In the next 20 minutes”

Specific time reduces nervous-system noise.

3.1.7 What individuals can do when pressure spikes (self-support)

This is for humans, not superheroes:

  • Name the pressure “This is financial pressure.”
    “This is belonging pressure.”
    Naming reduces the fog.

  • Shrink the promise Don’t promise “finish.” Promise “start.” Two-minute landing beats a two-hour guilt spiral.

  • Lower the stakes on the first draft “This is Draft Zero. It can be ugly.” Ugly drafts are how good work gets born.

  • Externalize uncertainty Write down what you don’t know yet. Turn vague fear into a list you can attack.

  • Ask for clarity early Anxiety loves silence. A 30-second question can save a 3-hour spiral.

3.1.8 A teaching/leadership note: pressure isn’t always bad

Some pressure is just importance. The goal isn’t to remove all pressure. The goal is to remove unnecessary threat: - shame threat - surprise threat - ambiguity threat - identity threat

When people feel safe enough to try, they become brave enough to learn.

3.2 Stress: a brain optimized for threats, not term projects

Under stress: - the brain wants certainty fast
- it grabs easy rewards
- it avoids ambiguous effort

CS work is the opposite of easy certainty: - debugging is ambiguous
- design choices are uncertain
- solutions take time to incubate

So stressed brains flee into: - scrolling
- “research” (that never ends)
- rearranging notes
- cleaning code that doesn’t need cleaning
- opening 37 tabs and calling it progress

3.3 Distraction: the attention economy is literally engineered

Phones, notifications, infinite feeds—these aren’t “weakness tests.” They’re slot machines in your pocket.

So Pomodoro becomes an attention firewall: - a small, defended window
- with a clear start and stop
- that you can repeat

4) The baby-steps ramp (how to build up to 25/5 without face-planting)

If someone is currently functioning in 30-second bursts of attention, demanding 25 minutes is like asking a couch to run a 5K.

So we ramp.

4.1 Level 0: “The Two-Minute Landing”

Goal: prove you can start. - Set a timer for 2 minutes - Do the smallest possible concrete action - open the file - run the tests - write the function signature - list the next 3 steps

Stop at 2 minutes on purpose.
This builds trust: starting is survivable.

4.2 Level 1: 5/2

  • 5 minutes work
  • 2 minutes break

4.3 Level 2: 10/3

  • 10 minutes work
  • 3 minutes break

4.4 Level 3: 15/5

  • 15 minutes work
  • 5 minutes break

4.5 Level 4: Classic 25/5

  • 25 minutes work
  • 5 minutes break
  • After 4 rounds: longer break

Rule: move up a level only after you can do the current one without suffering a morale collapse.

5) How to do a Pomodoro correctly (the “don’t accidentally ruin it” guide)

5.1 Choose a single target

Bad: “Work on homework.”
Good: “Write parse_input() and test it with 3 examples.”

5.2 Make interruptions visible (not fatal)

Keep a tiny “distraction log” during the sprint: - “Email professor” - “Look up regex” - “Text mom” - “Check Canvas”

Write it down. Don’t do it.
Your brain relaxes because it trusts you won’t forget.

5.3 Protect the break (don’t turn it into a second job)

Breaks should restore you, not drain you.

Good breaks: - stand up, stretch, drink water - quick walk - stare out a window (seriously) - breathe slow, loosen shoulders

Risky breaks: - social media (often becomes a trapdoor) - email (emotionally spiky) - “just one YouTube video” (famous last words)

5.4 End the sprint with a “resume hook”

Before the timer rings (or right after): - write one line: “Next, I will…” This eliminates the “restart pain” next round.

6) The problems people have with Pomodoro (and why it fails for them)

Pomodoro is simple. Humans are… creatively complicated.

Problem A: “25 minutes is too long / too short”

  • Too long: attention fatigue, anxiety spikes
  • Too short: deep work gets chopped up

Fix: customize the interval. Common alternatives: - 15/5 for beginners
- 30/5 or 45/10 for deeper focus
- 60/10 for advanced flow states
Pomodoro is a template, not a commandment.

Problem B: “I keep breaking focus anyway”

This isn’t failure; it’s data.

Common causes: - no clear target (“work on project” is fog) - environment is noisy - phone within reach - emotional avoidance (task feels threatening)

Fix: shrink target + reduce friction + externalize distractions.

Problem C: “Breaks make me lose momentum”

Some people hate stopping once they’re in flow.

Fix options: - Use Pomodoro mainly for starting, not for stopping. - If flow hits, allow “flow extension”: finish the current thought, then break. - Use longer intervals once you’ve built reliability.

Problem D: “It feels childish / mechanical”

That’s pride talking. Pride is allergic to training wheels.

Reframe:
This is not a toy; it’s a protocol.
Pilots use checklists. Athletes use intervals. Engineers use constraints.

Problem E: “My work doesn’t chunk nicely”

Some tasks are bursty and interrupt-driven (support tickets, lab monitoring).

Fix: use Pomodoro for: - planning the next chunk - batching admin tasks - carving one protected block per day for “real work”

Problem F: “I feel guilty during breaks”

Students think breaks are “cheating.”
But breaks are part of the system.

Reframe:
A break is not a reward. It’s maintenance.
Even servers need reboots. (Preferably scheduled ones.)

7) Support tools and companion habits (what makes Pomodoro actually stick)

Pomodoro works best when paired with a few allies:

7.1 A task menu (so you don’t waste the sprint choosing)

Have a short list of “next doable actions,” not vague goals.

Example menu (CS student): - implement Node class fields - write 5 unit tests for edge cases - fix off-by-one in loop - draft README usage examples

7.2 A definition of “done for now”

Perfectionism kills sprints.

Use “good enough for this round” checkpoints: - compiles - tests pass - explanation draft exists - commit message written

7.3 Environment cues

  • phone face down across the room
  • notifications off
  • full-screen editor
  • one monitor for code, one for instructions (not Discord)

7.4 A shutdown ritual

End of day: - write tomorrow’s first “2-minute landing” step
This turns tomorrow from dread into a doorway.

8) Serious limitations of Pomodoro (what it cannot fix)

Pomodoro is powerful—but it’s not magic.

8.1 It does not replace sleep, nutrition, movement

If a student is running on 4 hours of sleep and caffeine vapor, Pomodoro is like polishing a car with no engine.

8.2 It doesn’t solve unclear goals

If you don’t know what “success” looks like, you’ll sprint in circles.

8.3 It can clash with deep flow work

Some work benefits from long, uninterrupted immersion.
Rigid timers can interrupt insight.

8.4 It can become procrastination in disguise

People sometimes “optimize the system” instead of doing the work: - perfect timer apps - aesthetic planners - 19 productivity videos
No actual output.

8.5 It can amplify anxiety if framed as performance

If students treat each Pomodoro like a test, it becomes stressful. It should feel like a small promise kept, not a courtroom.

8.6 It won’t fix structural overload

If the workload is genuinely too large, Pomodoro helps triage—but the underlying problem remains.

9) Teaching Pomodoro to computer science majors (what to watch for)

CS majors have special strengths—and special traps.

9.1 Strength: they like systems

If you frame Pomodoro as: - a scheduling algorithm for attention - a throughput tool - a rate-limiting mechanism against distraction
…they’ll lean in.

9.2 Trap: they will over-engineer it

They will want to build: - a Pomodoro CLI - a Pomodoro web app - a Pomodoro distributed microservice with Kubernetes
…instead of doing the assignment.

Teaching move:
“Use a timer first. Automate later as extra credit.”

9.3 Trap: they confuse “time spent” with “progress”

A student can do 8 Pomodoros and still avoid the hard part.

Teaching move: require a tiny artifact per sprint: - a commit - a test - a paragraph explaining a concept - a screenshot of passing output - a bullet list of what changed and why

9.4 Trap: debugging doesn’t respect timers

Debugging can take 3 minutes or 3 hours.

Teaching move: Pomodoro works great for debugging if you define the sprint as: - “form a hypothesis” - “run one experiment” - “log what I learned” That turns thrash into science.

9.5 Trap: group work + misaligned rhythms

Pair programming and group projects can’t always sync.

Teaching move: use “team pomodoros”: - 20 minutes collaboration - 5 minutes notes and decision log - 20 minutes implement - 5 minutes review

9.6 Concern: some students have ADHD/anxiety accommodations

Timers can help some and stress others.

Teaching stance: - present Pomodoro as an option, not a requirement - encourage flexible intervals - emphasize self-observation over compliance

10) A classroom-friendly script (what you can say out loud)

“You don’t need motivation. You need a starting ritual.
The timer is just a gate that says: for a little while, we do one thing.
If 25 minutes feels too big, we don’t fight ourselves—we scale the sprint.
Two minutes. Five minutes. Ten. Fifteen. Then twenty-five.
We are not trying to become robots. We are trying to become reliable.”

11) Discussion prompts (for students, reflection, or class chat)

  • What is your biggest distraction: phone, people, anxiety, or uncertainty?
  • Which is harder for you: starting or staying?
  • What interval feels doable right now: 5, 10, 15, 25?
  • What is a “safe break” for you that won’t trap you?
  • What does “done for now” look like on your current assignment?
  • If you did 4 sprints on this project, what would be different by tonight?

12) Quick “Pomodoro Starter Pack” (copy/paste)

My next sprint target: ______
Timer: ___ minutes work / ___ minutes break
If distracted, I will write it here:
- ______
- ______
At the end of this sprint, the next step is: _____

13) Closing thought (because your brain deserves some poetry)

You are not a machine built to run forever.
You are a creature of breath and rhythm.
Pomodoro is a metronome for your attention—
not to cage you,
but to help you return.

One sprint at a time, you build a life that ships.

pages.title: Mindfulness Module
pages.body:
Mindfulness Module

Generated from: 02_weeks\W01\05_mindfulness_module.md

1) Origins: where mindfulness comes from (two streams)

1.1 The contemplative stream (ancient)

In early Buddhist traditions, mindfulness (sati) is central to practice, often framed as “establishing mindfulness” across body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena (the classic “foundations of mindfulness”). (Access to Insight)

If you teach this in a classroom, you don’t need the full spiritual frame—just the universal human problem it addresses:

Minds wander. Minds worry. Minds react. Mindfulness trains noticing—so you can respond instead of reflex.

1.2 The modern clinical stream (secular + evidence-based)

In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn created Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) at UMass as an 8-week program—bringing contemplative practices into mainstream medicine with a secular, practical approach. (UMass Memorial Health)

This matters for students because it’s a translation:

  • from monastery to hospital to classroom
  • from “mystical” to “trainable”

2) A key twist: Ellen Langer’s “mindfulness without meditation”

A lot of students hear “mindfulness” and assume “sitting still, chanting, becoming a monk.” Langer flips that.

Ellen Langer defines mindfulness as “actively noticing new things.” (Psychwire) That means you can practice mindfulness while walking, coding, eating, talking, debugging—by noticing differences, details, and change.

This is huge for CS majors because it reframes mindfulness as:

  • better observation
  • better debugging
  • better decision-making under uncertainty

3) The nursing home + plants study: why it’s so famous

In a classic 1976 field experiment in a nursing home, residents in the “enhanced responsibility + choice” group were:

  • given a message emphasizing their responsibility for themselves
  • given more choices
  • and given responsibility for caring for a plant (instead of staff caring for it) (PubMed)

Results: the experimental group showed improvement in alertness, active participation, and a general sense of well-being compared with the comparison group. (PubMed)

A follow-up paper reported sustained benefits 18 months later, using nurse ratings and health/mortality indicators. (PubMed)

The “why it works” lesson (for students)

This wasn’t “positive vibes.” It was agency.

When humans feel:

  • no control
  • no choices
  • no responsibility that matters

…the nervous system often slides toward passivity.

Mindfulness (Langer-style) is a way of giving the brain back a tiny lever:

“I can notice. I can choose. I can steer.”

That lever is small—yet it changes everything.

4) Meng at Google: Joy on Demand + “Everyday Compassion”

Chade-Meng Tan (“Meng”) helped bring mindfulness into workplace culture through Search Inside Yourself (SIY)—a program developed at Google beginning in 2007 to strengthen emotional intelligence and resilience. (siyli.org)

He also gave a widely shared talk, “Everyday Compassion at Google.” (YouTube) And he later taught themes from Joy on Demand in a Google talk (“Talks at Google”). (YouTube)

4.1 Meng’s “Joy on Demand” idea in one sentence

Joy isn’t only something that happens to you—it’s also something you can train access to, like a skill.

Not constant happiness. Not denial. More like: a reliable ability to shift your mind-state when you need it most.

5) Why mindfulness works (the mechanics, not the mythology)

Here’s the clean “CS-friendly” model:

5.1 Attention is a resource (and you can train it)

Mindfulness is reps for attention:

  • you notice wandering
  • you return
  • you repeat

That loop is literally the workout.

5.2 Awareness creates “space” between stimulus and response

Without mindfulness:

  • feeling → reaction → regret

With mindfulness:

  • feeling → noticing → choice → better outcome

That “space” is where good decisions live.

5.3 Your body is the fastest door into your nervous system

Breath, posture, muscle tension—these are not “woo.” They’re inputs to your stress response.

A slower exhale tends to cue “we’re safe enough right now,” which makes thinking easier.

5.4 Joy and compassion aren’t “extra”—they’re stabilizers

When your mind is flooded with threat, it narrows. When your mind has warmth (toward self and others), it widens.

Joy isn’t fluff; it’s cognitive climate control.

6) How students can start with “half a breath”

Yes. Half. Not 20 minutes. Not incense. Not a mountaintop. Half a breath is small enough that nobody’s ego can complain.

6.1 The Half-Breath Reset (5–10 seconds)

  1. Exhale… just a little longer than normal. (That’s the “half.”)
  2. Notice one sensation: feet on floor, hands on desk, air at nostrils.
  3. Quietly label: “here.”
  4. Ask: “What’s the next tiny step?”

That’s it. You just interrupted autopilot.

6.2 The “One Line of Code” version (for CS brains)

Before you touch the keyboard:

  • half-breath
  • then decide: What is the next line I’m writing?
  • then write only that line

Mindfulness becomes a launch button.

6.3 The 3-Ping Practice (30 seconds)

Do three quick notices:

  • Body: one sensation
  • Mind: one thought (name it: “planning,” “worrying,” “judging”)
  • Task: one next action

This turns “vague stress” into “structured motion.”

7) How to teach mindfulness without triggering eye-rolls in CS majors

7.1 Frame it as performance + agency, not spirituality

Say something like:

“This is attention training for people who do hard things under uncertainty.”

7.2 Make it measurable

Give them data hooks:

  • number of resets per class
  • time-to-start on a hard problem
  • ability to return after distraction

7.3 Keep practices tiny and optional

Mandatory deep meditation can backfire. Tiny defaults work better:

  • half-breath resets
  • 30-second 3-Ping
  • mindful “start” ritual for labs

7.4 Tie it to debugging and proof-writing

Mindfulness skills map cleanly to:

  • noticing assumptions
  • spotting cognitive loops
  • slowing down before a bad commit
  • tolerating ambiguity long enough to solve it

8) Common misunderstandings + limitations (teach this honestly)

8.1 “Mindfulness means I should feel calm.”

Nope. Mindfulness means you notice what’s true—calm or not.

8.2 “If I’m still anxious, it’s not working.”

Also nope. Often it’s working because you’re noticing what was always there.

8.3 Not a cure-all

Mindfulness can be supportive, but it’s not a substitute for professional care when someone is dealing with severe anxiety, depression, trauma responses, or panic. (Teach it as a tool, not a diagnosis.)

8.4 Some students may feel worse at first

When you slow down, you might notice discomfort you were avoiding. So give them a safety valve:

  • eyes open is fine
  • focus on feet/hands instead of breath
  • stop anytime, no explanations required

9) A ready-to-use classroom script (2 minutes)

“Before we start: we’re doing a half-breath reset. Exhale slightly longer than usual… Notice one sensation—feet, hands, air—anything. Label it: ‘here.’ Now ask: ‘What’s my next tiny step?’

That’s mindfulness: noticing + choosing. We’re not trying to become monks. We’re trying to become less hackable by distraction and stress.”

10) Tiny challenges (so this becomes real)

Week 1: “3 resets per class”

Students do:

  • half-breath reset at start
  • one reset when stuck
  • one reset before turning something in

Week 2: “Mindful debugging”

When something fails:

  1. half-breath
  2. write one sentence: “What do I know for sure?”
  3. write one hypothesis
  4. run one test

That’s mindfulness as engineering.

Source anchors (for you, instructor)

  • Langer & Rodin nursing home experiment included plant care + choice/responsibility; improved alertness/participation/well-being. (PubMed)
  • Follow-up reported sustained benefits at ~18 months using health/mortality indicators. (PubMed)
  • Langer’s mindfulness: “actively noticing new things.” (Psychwire)
  • MBSR created by Kabat-Zinn in 1979 at UMass. (UMass Memorial Health)
  • SIY origins at Google beginning in 2007; widely used mindfulness-at-work program. (siyli.org)
  • Meng’s “Everyday Compassion at Google” talk is available via YouTube. (YouTube)

If you want, paste your Discrete Structures Day 1 plan and I’ll splice this into a tight lecture flow: 5-minute story hook (plants), 2-minute practice (half-breath), 5-minute “why it works,” and a 1-slide “CS translation” so it lands with your majors.

pages.title: Scarcity vs Surplus (Abundance) — What Fear Does to the Mind
pages.body:
Lecture Module: Scarcity vs Surplus (Abundance) — What Fear Does to the Mind

Lecture Module: Scarcity vs Surplus (Abundance) — What Fear Does to the Mind

Audience: Humans (especially CS students under deadline pressure)
Purpose: Explain scarcity mindset vs surplus mindset, why each happens, how it affects cognition, and how to build healthier habits without ignoring real constraints.

1) The Core Question

Why do some people live like the world is always about to run out—time, money, attention, love, safety—while others move through life like there will be enough, and so they can be generous?

This isn’t just “attitude.” It’s often nervous system + history + environment + learned strategy.

2) Definitions (simple and useful)

Scarcity mindset

A mental state where the brain is convinced:

  • there won’t be enough
  • I have to protect what I have
  • if I relax, I’ll lose
  • if I fall behind, I won’t recover

Scarcity can be triggered by real conditions (poverty, instability, trauma, illness), or by perceived conditions (comparison, uncertainty, perfectionism, high-stakes environments).

Surplus (abundance) mindset

A mental state where the brain is convinced:

  • I can recover
  • resources can be replenished
  • I can share without collapsing
  • I have enough margin to breathe and think

Surplus is not “delusion.” It’s felt safety + margin + trust.

3) What Scarcity Does to the Mind (the “tunnel” effect)

When people feel scarcity, the brain does something predictable:

3.1 Attention tunnels

Scarcity pulls attention toward the “urgent threat”:

  • “I’m behind.”
  • “I’m going to fail.”
  • “I’m running out of time.”
  • “I can’t mess this up.”

This tunneling can create:

  • hyper-focus on immediate tasks
  • difficulty seeing long-term plans
  • reduced ability to switch contexts cleanly

3.2 Working memory shrinks

Fear eats mental bandwidth. It’s like trying to debug while your computer is also running a full virus scan.

Symptoms:

  • forgetting steps
  • losing track of what you tried
  • rereading the same paragraph 6 times
  • making impulsive choices just to end discomfort

3.3 Executive function gets expensive

Planning, prioritizing, and resisting distraction require energy. Scarcity makes those skills cost more.

So people default to:

  • quick rewards (scrolling, snacking, distractions)
  • avoidance (“I’ll start later”)
  • over-control (perfectionism, micromanaging)

3.4 Social behavior contracts

Scarcity often reduces generosity—not because someone is selfish, but because the brain says:

“If I give, I might not survive.”

This can look like:

  • less patience
  • less collaboration
  • more defensiveness
  • more “keeping score”

3.5 The cruel loop

Scarcity makes it harder to make good decisions, which can lead to worse outcomes, which increases scarcity.

That loop is why shame is such a bad teacher.

4) What Surplus Does to the Mind (the “wide angle” effect)

4.1 Cognitive flexibility increases

Surplus supports:

  • creativity
  • learning
  • problem-solving
  • perspective-taking

You can hold multiple ideas without panicking.

4.2 Long-term planning becomes possible

Surplus makes it easier to:

  • start early
  • break tasks into chunks
  • recover from mistakes
  • invest in skills that pay off later

4.3 Generosity becomes rational

When you trust you can recover, generosity stops feeling like danger. You can share time, attention, knowledge, encouragement, and resources.

And generosity tends to strengthen relationships—which increases support—which increases felt surplus. That’s the “good spiral.”

5) Why Surplus is a Good Idea (and also why it’s hard)

Why it’s a good idea

Surplus mindset tends to produce:

  • better thinking
  • better relationships
  • better resilience after failure
  • more consistent progress
  • less desperation-driven decision-making

In a CS context, surplus supports the ability to calmly do the real work:

  • read carefully
  • test hypotheses
  • debug systematically
  • ask for help early
  • collaborate without ego fights

Why it’s a challenge

Surplus isn’t a slogan. It requires at least one of these:

  • Real resources (money, time, stable housing, reliable support)
  • Real margin (buffers, slack, recovery plans)
  • Real safety (psychological safety, predictable rules, dignity)
  • Real repetition (evidence that “I can recover” becomes believable)

If a person is truly in scarcity, telling them “just think abundant thoughts” can feel insulting. Surplus mindset is easiest when the environment supports it.

6) The Big Warning: Don’t turn “abundance” into blame

Some people are in real, structural scarcity. They are not “failing at mindset.” They are adapting to reality.

A healthy classroom message is:

“We respect real constraints.
We build tiny buffers where we can.
We avoid creating unnecessary threat.
We practice surplus in ways that don’t deny reality.”

7) How Students Can Start Building Surplus (even if life is chaotic)

Surplus begins with micro-margin: tiny pockets of safety.

7.1 The “Half-Breath + Wide-Angle” reset (10 seconds)

  1. Exhale slightly longer than normal
  2. Look away from the screen and notice three things in the room
  3. Ask: “What is the smallest next action?”

This interrupts tunnel vision.

7.2 Build a 15-minute “buffer block”

Once per day, schedule 15 minutes that is not for doing tasks—only for:

  • planning tomorrow
  • catching up on one tiny thing
  • asking one question
  • cleaning one mess
  • making one “future me” gift

This is how you manufacture margin in a life that doesn’t provide it.

7.3 The “Generosity without collapse” rule

Generosity doesn’t mean draining yourself dry. Teach students to be generous with boundaries.

Offer help in small, repeatable units:

  • “I can help for 10 minutes.”
  • “I can explain one concept.”
  • “I can review one function.”
  • “I can point you to the right resource.”

7.4 Replace “I’m behind” with “What’s next”

“I’m behind” is a scarcity spell. “What’s next” is a surplus question.

7.5 The anti-scarcity workflow for assignments

  1. Define “done for now”
  2. Find the smallest deliverable
  3. Do one short sprint (Pomodoro or mini-sprint)
  4. Leave a “resume hook” (one sentence: “Next I will…”)

Consistency builds safety.

8) Teaching this to CS majors (how to make it land)

8.1 Translate into systems language

  • Scarcity = low bandwidth, high interrupt load, no cache, constant paging
  • Surplus = enough RAM to reason, plan, and run multiple processes safely

8.2 Reward process artifacts (not panic hours)

Ask for:

  • commits
  • test logs
  • short debug journals (“hypothesis → experiment → result”)
  • checklists

That reduces the “all-or-nothing” scarcity vibe.

8.3 Don’t weaponize deadlines

Deadlines matter, but “doom language” spikes tunnel vision. Use predictable rules + recovery paths:

  • partial credit for early drafts
  • revision windows
  • checkpoints
  • clear rubrics

This encourages learning rather than hiding.

9) Discussion prompts

  • Where do you feel scarcity most: time, money, attention, belonging, confidence?
  • What does scarcity make you do that you later regret?
  • What does surplus make possible in your best weeks?
  • What’s one tiny buffer you could build this week?
  • What is a generous action you can take that won’t collapse you?

10) A short closing script

“Scarcity makes the mind tunnel.
Surplus gives the mind a wide lens.

We’re not pretending life is easy.
We’re building tiny pockets of margin—so our brains can do what they do best: learn, solve, and connect.

Your goal is not to become endlessly calm.
Your goal is to become recoverable.
When you believe you can recover, you can be brave.
And when you can be brave, you can build.”

End of module.

pages.title: STAR Bullets: Turn Duties Into Evidence
pages.body:
STAR Bullets: Turn Duties Into Evidence

STAR Bullets: Turn Duties Into Evidence

A reference page you can return to anytime while building your resume.

Today’s Big Idea

You are not “hoping” your future works out — you’re building it on purpose.
Today we turn vague effort into evidence.

Resume mindset: Your resume is not a diary. It’s a proof document.

STAR Bullets (Achievement bullets, not duty bullets)

Core idea

You get to build your story on purpose (skills, projects, evidence).

The shift: Duties → Achievements

Duty bullets describe what you were around.

Achievement bullets describe what you accomplished and what changed because of it.

Duty (weak)

  • Helped customers
  • Worked on a team project
  • Used Python

Achievement (strong)

  • Resolved 15+ customer issues per shift, improving satisfaction and reducing manager escalations.
  • Collaborated with a 4-person team to deliver a working prototype by deadline, documenting decisions and test results.
  • Built a Python script to automate file cleanup, saving ~30 minutes per week.

STAR in one breath

  • S/T (Situation/Task): context in one short phrase
  • A (Action): a strong verb (built, analyzed, designed, led…)
  • R (Result): the “so what?” ideally with numbers

Bullet formula

[Power Verb] + [What you did / context] + [Result/benefit]

Two fast examples

  • “Resolved 15+ customer issues per shift, improving satisfaction and reducing manager escalations.”
  • “Built a Python script to automate file cleanup, saving ~30 minutes per week.”

How to write stronger STAR bullets (quick tips)

1) Use a power verb that matches what you did

Built, Designed, Implemented, Analyzed, Optimized, Automated, Debugged, Led, Coordinated, Documented, Presented, Trained, Resolved

2) Add “proof” whenever possible

Proof can be:

  • Numbers: time saved, errors reduced, tickets handled, accuracy improved
  • Scale: number of users, team size, dataset size, project scope
  • Artifacts: GitHub repo, demo video, screenshots, documentation, write-up
  • Constraints: short deadline, limited resources, unclear requirements, messy data

3) Make the result real

If you don’t have a perfect metric, use a reasonable one:

  • reduced rework
  • improved reliability
  • increased clarity
  • saved time weekly
  • reduced confusion for new users

Build Your Resume Evidence Bank

What counts as evidence?

  • Numbers: time saved, errors reduced, volume handled, speed improved
  • Scale: people served, files processed, tickets closed, pages written
  • Artifacts: GitHub repo, screenshots, write-ups, documentation, demos
  • Constraints: deadlines, limited resources, no admin access, messy data

Evidence prompts

Pick 3 and answer in short phrases:

  • What did I make?
  • What did I fix?
  • What did I improve?
  • What problem did I notice and solve?
  • What did I do that saved time, reduced stress, or increased quality?

Pro move: Keep a running “Evidence Notes” document. Add one win per week. Future-you will thank present-you like it’s a holiday.

Resume Overview: What you should be building this semester

What the resume must show

  • Skills (tools + concepts)
  • Evidence (STAR bullets, projects, results)
  • Direction (where you’re headed and how you’re preparing)

Minimum “resume progress” expectation (by end of Week 2)

  • 5–8 STAR bullets drafted (mix of school + work + life)
  • 1 project artifact link (GitHub repo or a document/demo)
  • Skills section that matches your evidence (no “fantasy skills”)

Formatting tips for automated resume systems (ATS-friendly)

Many employers use Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) that scan resumes automatically. The goal: make your resume easy for robots and humans to read.

Do this (ATS-friendly)

  • Use a clean, single-column layout.
  • Use standard section headings: Education, Experience, Projects, Skills, Certifications, Leadership/Activities.
  • Use simple fonts (avoid fancy/script fonts).
  • Use consistent formatting for dates and titles.
  • Export as PDF unless the posting requests DOCX.
  • Match keywords from the job posting honestly (tools/languages/concepts you actually used).
  • Put key skills in Skills and reinforce them in bullets with evidence.

Avoid this (ATS-unfriendly)

  • Tables, text boxes, columns, or complex templates
  • Graphics-heavy resumes, icons, or skill bars
  • Headers/footers containing critical info (some systems miss them)
  • Images of text (ATS can’t read it reliably)
  • Over-stylized section titles (keep headings standard)

Keywords without lying

ATS looks for keywords, humans look for evidence:

  • Don’t just list “Python” — prove it with a bullet.
  • If you used a tool in class, include it in Projects, Skills, and in a bullet.

File naming (tiny detail, big professionalism)

  • LastName_FirstName_Resume.pdf
  • Evert_Jeremy_Resume.pdf

Notes / Reminders

  • Your resume is not a diary. It’s a proof document.
  • Each week you add one proof item.
  • Consistency beats hero mode. (Hero mode is a liar with good marketing.)

Keep this page bookmarked. When you’re stuck, come back, pick one prompt, and write one bullet. That’s how resumes get built — one proof brick at a time.

pages.title: SMART Goals (and Beyond): How to Set Goals That Actually Work
pages.body:
SMART Goals (and Beyond): How to Set Goals That Actually Work

SMART Goals (and Beyond): How to Set Goals That Actually Work

A reference page you can come back to whenever your goals start getting foggy.

The awkward truth about goals

Most goals don’t fail because you “didn’t want it enough.” They fail because the goal was never designed to survive real life.

Real life includes stress, busy weeks, missed days, surprise responsibilities, low energy, limited time, imperfect motivation— and that one week where everything catches fire at once.

Why goals fail (common patterns)

1) The goal is too vague

  • “Get better at math.”
  • “Be more organized.”
  • “Study more.”
  • “Be healthier.”

Vague goals don’t answer: what exactly do you do, how often, how do you measure progress, and when are you done?

2) The goal is too big to start

Big goals can be great long-term visions, but if they don’t break down into something you can do this week, they become intimidation monuments.

3) The goal is based on feelings, not systems

Motivation is a weather pattern. Goals that depend on motivation eventually become goals you “used to have.”

4) The goal is unrealistic for your current life

Unrealistic goals don’t make you strong—they make you quit. A good goal fits your actual schedule.

5) The goal lacks relevance

If it isn’t tied to what matters to you right now, it won’t stick once it gets hard.

6) The goal has no deadline

A goal without a time boundary becomes “Someday I’ll…” and someday is a magical land where nothing ever happens.

7) The goal is all outcome, no process

Outcome goals are fine, but process goals are what you control.

8) The goal ignores setbacks

A fragile goal collapses when you miss one day. A good goal has a built-in reset plan.

What SMART goals do (and what problem they solve)

SMART goals are a tool that solves three big problems:

  • Confusion: SMART goals make the goal clear enough to act on.
  • No feedback loop: SMART goals define measurement so you can adjust instead of guessing.
  • No finish line: SMART goals create a deadline, turning “someday” into “by this date.”

SMART doesn’t magically make you disciplined. It makes your goal well-built so your discipline has something real to attach to.

What SMART stands for (with real meaning)

S Specific

Define exactly what you’re doing. The next step should be obvious.

M Measurable

Create a scoreboard: problems solved, minutes studied, commits pushed, drafts submitted, accuracy improved.

A Achievable

Challenging but possible, sustainable in your current life. Not easy—just realistic.

R Relevant

The goal matters right now and connects to priorities: class outcomes, career direction, real needs.

T Time-bound

A deadline creates clarity, urgency, and a moment to reflect and reset.

Good characteristics of SMART goals

  • Actionable: uses real verbs (write, solve, submit, build).
  • Small enough to start: includes a minimum effective action.
  • Has a scoreboard: evidence you can point at.
  • Has a real deadline: a date, not “soon.”
  • Adjustable: you can refactor instead of quitting.

Strong SMART goals (good examples)

Example 1: Academic skill building

Goal: By February 13, I will complete 24 discrete math practice problems (~3/week) and track accuracy in a simple log, aiming to raise accuracy from ~60% to 80%.

Why it’s good: clear task, measurable count, realistic pace, relevant impact, clear deadline.

Example 2: Writing and communication

Goal: By February 6, I will produce two polished STAR bullet drafts each week (total 6 bullets) and revise them using feedback from one peer or the instructor.

Why it’s good: steady cadence, concrete output, includes feedback loop, time-bound.

Example 3: Project momentum

Goal: By March 1, I will publish a small GitHub project with at least 10 meaningful commits, a README, and a demo screenshot or short video, using two 45-minute sessions per week.

Why it’s good: clear deliverables, measurable, scheduled time blocks, portfolio-ready.

Example 4: Support systems

Goal: From now until Exam 1 (Feb 20), I will attend one office hour/tutoring session per week and bring two specific questions based on my practice work.

Why it’s good: builds a habit + accountability, measurable, highly relevant.

Bad examples (and why they fail) + refactors (how to fix them)

Bad: “Study more.”

  • Why it’s bad: vague, not measurable, no deadline, no next action.
  • Refactor: By Feb 13, I will complete 3 discrete math practice problems per week and log completion and accuracy (12 total).

Bad: “Get an A in this class.”

  • Why it’s bad: outcome-only; no controllable process; feedback may come too late.
  • Refactor: By Exam 1 (Feb 20), I will do two Pomodoro sessions of practice weekly and attend one help session weekly, aiming for 80%+ on quizzes.

Bad: “Stop procrastinating.”

  • Why it’s bad: negative and slippery; not measurable; creates guilt instead of action.
  • Refactor: For 14 days, I will start homework with a 10-minute “starter block” within 24 hours of assignment, tracking starts (goal: 10 starts).

Bad: “Be healthier.”

  • Why it’s bad: too broad; not measurable; no plan; no deadline.
  • Refactor: By Feb 13, I will complete 3 workouts/week (20–30 minutes) and average 6,000 steps/day tracked by phone/watch.

Bad: “Learn Python.”

  • Why it’s bad: huge scope; unclear finish line; not measurable.
  • Refactor: By March 1, I will complete 8 beginner Python exercises (2/week) and publish solutions to GitHub with brief explanations.

Pitfalls to avoid (even with SMART)

  • Too complicated: If tracking is harder than doing, you’ll stop. Keep it simple.
  • Fantasy goals: Goals designed for a life you don’t currently have. Build for your real schedule.
  • Activity ≠ progress: Time spent isn’t always improvement. Use feedback loops (practice + review mistakes).
  • Punishment goals: If it feels like a cage, you’ll rebel. Make goals supportive.
  • No reset plan: Add a rule: “missed day → restart tomorrow; missed week → shrink and rebuild.”

Beyond SMART: what “good goals” are made of

1) Balance outcome goals and process goals

Outcome gives direction. Process creates progress.

2) Design goals for identity (who you’re becoming)

Ask: “Who do I want to become?” Consistent behavior builds identity.

3) Use constraints as allies

Constraints are design requirements. Build goals that fit your available time and energy.

4) Your environment is part of your plan

Set a study location, remove distractions, pre-load materials, and use a timer.

5) Celebrate small wins

Celebration isn’t cheesy—it’s reinforcement that makes consistency easier.

A few concepts inspired by Michael Hyatt (“Your Best Year Ever”-style thinking)

Adapted and summarized for classroom use—ideas, not quotes.

1) Write goals down and keep them visible

A goal that only lives in your head disappears when your week gets busy.

2) Motivation follows progress

Don’t wait for motivation—create a small win (10 minutes of progress, one problem solved, one draft started).

3) Believe change is possible, but don’t rely on hype

Optimism helps. Structure makes it real. SMART gives structure.

4) Focus on a few goals that matter

Too many goals dilutes effort. Aim for 1–3 major goals at a time.

5) Build support and accountability

Peer check-ins, tutoring, instructor feedback, and study groups create traction.

Quick template: build your own SMART goal

By (date), I will (specific action) (how often/how much),
and I will measure it by (tracker/evidence), because it supports (why it matters).

Example: By Feb 13, I will complete 3 practice problems per week and track accuracy in a spreadsheet, because it supports Exam 1 performance.

Final reminder

A SMART goal is not a magic spell. It’s a well-built tool. When life gets messy (it will), the goal isn’t “be perfect.” The goal is: keep building.

Tip: When your goals wobble, don’t panic—shrink the goal, rebuild momentum, and keep going.

pages.title: 3-2-1 Journaling: A Tiny Daily Habit That Builds a Big Life
pages.body:
3-2-1 Journaling: A Tiny Daily Habit That Builds a Big Life

3-2-1 Journaling: A Tiny Daily Habit That Builds a Big Life

Daily capture → weekly expansion → monthly resume update. A pipeline for turning life into evidence.

The Big Idea

Most people do a lot… and then forget it. Days blur. Weeks evaporate. Months vanish. And when it’s time to write a resume, apply for an internship, or explain your growth, your brain turns into a blank loading screen.

3-2-1 turns your daily life into a searchable archive of proof—and a steady pipeline of resume material.

What 3-2-1 means

  • 3 Daily (≤ 5 minutes): Record three things you did today.
  • 2 Weekly (one Pomodoro): Choose two daily entries and expand them into longer story paragraphs.
  • 1 Monthly (one Pomodoro sprint): Add one new line to your resume using your weekly stories as source material.

Workflow: Daily capture → Weekly expansion → Monthly resume update.

Translation: you stop relying on memory and start relying on receipts.

The alarm + voice-to-text workflow (how to actually do it)

Step 1: Set two alarms

Set an alarm for Start and Stop — exactly 5 minutes apart.

  • The first alarm gets you started.
  • The second alarm keeps you from overthinking or spiraling into perfectionism.

Step 2: Open your phone and record

  • Open a recording app or voice-to-text.
  • Talk into a document.
  • Start with the date and the day of the week.

Example start: “Tuesday, January 14…”

Step 3: Say your 3 things (fast)

Say three things you did today. They can be class/work/personal/family—anything meaningful.

Goal: capture reality. Not fancy. Not perfect. Just true.

Why “three things you did today” is a power move

1) Your brain is bad at remembering your progress

Humans remember stress and emotion more easily than quiet wins. Without a record, your growth becomes invisible.

2) Small wins create momentum

When you can see yourself making progress, motivation gets easier. Progress becomes a healthy habit.

3) It builds self-trust

Self-trust is basically: “I do what I say I will do.” Recording your actions reinforces identity: “I’m a person who finishes things.”

4) It turns your life into evidence

This record feeds resumes, interviews, scholarships, letters of recommendation, and the moment you think “I haven’t done anything.”

You will have receipts.

Optional add-on: the “tomorrow seed”

Add one sentence at the end:

“One thing I want to accomplish tomorrow is…”

This reduces decision fatigue and gives future-you a clear starting point.

The “2” part: weekly expansion (Pomodoro + reflection)

After a week you’ll have 15–21 daily entries (or more). That list is gold.

Why weekly reflection matters

Daily entries are quick and raw. Weekly reflection is where you slow down, notice patterns, and convert notes into usable stories.

Weekly workflow (one good Pomodoro)

  1. Start a 25-minute Pomodoro.
  2. Skim your week of entries.
  3. Choose two entries with potential (something you improved, finished, solved, or learned).
  4. Expand one into a paragraph (if time remains, start the second).

What the paragraph should include (STAR-friendly)

  • Situation/Task: What was going on? What did you need to do?
  • Action: What steps did you take?
  • Result: What changed? What did you learn? Any numbers?

Why long-form matters: When you write the full story now, future-you won’t have to reconstruct it from scraps later.

Curriculum Vita: what it is (and why you want one)

A Curriculum Vita (often “CV”) is a longer record of your academic and professional life. A resume is a highlight reel. A CV is the vault.

Resume (highlight reel)

  • Short
  • Selective
  • Polished
  • Tailored to the job

Curriculum Vita (your vault)

  • Long-form
  • Everything-you’ve-done
  • Not pretty on purpose
  • Full of proof + story paragraphs

Your class version of a “CV vault” can include:

  • weekly story paragraphs
  • project notes and deliverables
  • problems solved and lessons learned
  • leadership moments
  • links to artifacts (repos, demos, docs)

When it’s time to apply for something, you don’t rely on memory. You go to the vault.

The “1” part: monthly resume sprint (one Pomodoro)

Once a month, schedule a 25-minute sprint to add one new resume line.

Where does the resume line come from?

  • Your weekly story paragraphs
  • Your CV vault entries

Why “one resume line per month” is huge

  • Your resume stays fresh.
  • You never build a resume from panic.
  • You steadily convert real work into polished evidence.

Preserve old content

When new things come in, old lines may get trimmed from the resume. That’s normal. But don’t delete history—move older content into your CV vault.

Why students benefit (the payoff)

  • Better interviews: you’ll have stories ready, not vague claims.
  • Better resumes: you’ll have evidence and STAR-ready content.
  • Better self-awareness: you’ll notice what energizes you and where you grow.
  • Better consistency: 5 minutes daily + 25 minutes weekly + 25 minutes monthly is sustainable.
  • Less anxiety: a record reduces “Where did my time go?” stress.

A sample 3-2-1 entry (quick model)

Wednesday, Jan 14
1) Finished the logic homework set and corrected two mistakes after checking solutions.
2) Helped a classmate understand contrapositive proofs using a simple example.
3) Started a GitHub repo for my project and made two commits with a basic README.
Tomorrow seed: Start the next problem set with a 10-minute starter block right after class.

Trust but verify: how this can go wrong (and how to fix it)

Failure mode 1: You turn it into a diary

Fix: Keep it evidence-based: what you did, what you learned, what you’ll do next.

Failure mode 2: You try to be perfect

Fix: Capture fast, messy truth. Your future self needs content, not perfection.

Failure mode 3: Your “three things” are always vague

Fix: Add one detail: topic, output, obstacle, result, or lesson learned.

Failure mode 4: You never do the weekly “2”

Fix: Put the weekly Pomodoro on your calendar like a real appointment.

Failure mode 5: You never do the monthly “1”

Fix: Choose a consistent monthly trigger (first Friday, last day of the month, etc.).

Failure mode 6: You use it like a guilt weapon

Fix: Treat it like brushing your teeth—small, routine, protective. Not dramatic.

Quick start checklist

  • Set two alarms: start + stop (5 minutes apart)
  • Create a running document: “3-2-1 Journal”
  • Daily: date + 3 things you did (≤5 minutes)
  • Weekly: one Pomodoro to expand 2 entries into story paragraphs
  • Create a “Curriculum Vita (Vault)” doc and store story paragraphs there
  • Monthly: one Pomodoro to add 1 new resume line

Final reminder

This isn’t about being impressive. It’s about being awake in your own life long enough to collect proof that you’re growing. Tiny habit. Big archive. Strong future.

Tip: If you miss a day, don’t restart your identity—restart your timer. One entry at a time.

Pick one problem from this week’s chapter

You may choose any example or problem from the textbook, or you may modify one.
Cite where it came from (section/page or problem #). If you changed it, briefly explain what you changed and why.

1) Sources (20 pts)

Do: List 2 edited sources (textbook, class notes, university resource).
Add: 1 short bullet per source: what you used from it.

  • 20: 2+ edited sources + clear “I used this” bullets
  • 15: 2 sources but bullets are vague
  • 8: only 1 edited source
  • 0: no real sources

2) Rules / Assumptions (20 pts)

Do: Write the few rules you had to decide so the problem is clear.

Use this format:

  • Must-do (from prompt): ___
  • I will assume/decide: ___ (1–3 bullets)
  • 20: must-do + 1–3 clear decisions that make the task doable
  • 15: mostly clear but missing one key decision
  • 8: vague or too many unnecessary rules
  • 0: missing, or rules contradict the prompt

3) Work (20 pts)

Do: Show your steps clearly enough that someone else could follow.

  • 20: clear, correct steps
  • 15: mostly correct, small mistakes/gaps
  • 8: some work, but missing big steps
  • 0: little/no meaningful work

4) Check Your Answer (20 pts)

Do: Do one quick check and explain it (1–3 sentences).

Pick one:

  • small example / test case
  • edge case
  • compare to definition/theorem
  • sanity check (“does this make sense?”)
  • 20: one real check that could catch errors
  • 15: check exists but is weak
  • 8: “I think it’s right” (no real check)
  • 0: nothing

5) One-Sentence Summary (20 pts)

Do: In one sentence, say what the question asked you to do.

  • 20: accurate + specific
  • 15: mostly right but vague
  • 8: unclear or partly wrong
  • 0: missing

Quick self-check

  • ☐ 2 edited sources
  • ☐ 1–3 rules/assumptions
  • ☐ work shown
  • ☐ one check
  • ☐ one-sentence summary
